Nothing in the conversation history says what those views were, so anything I wrote would put invented opinions in his mouth. That could easily be quoted or mistaken for something he really said. fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think I should be a little careful here, because "pessimistic" sounds harsher in hindsight than it felt at the time. It wasn't that I thought the company was going to fail. It was more that I was running a fairly simple mental model, and the model said the odds were against them.

The model went something like this. In the first half of AI, the thing that mattered most was raw scale: compute, data, the ability to train the biggest model. And on that axis Anthropic looked structurally disadvantaged. Less compute than OpenAI or Google, no consumer distribution to speak of, a smaller team, and a brand that most people outside the field associated with "safety" rather than "the best model." If you believe the game is decided by who has the most GPUs and the most users, that's a tough hand to play. I also worried that the safety emphasis, which I genuinely respected, would slow down shipping in a market where shipping speed was starting to matter a lot.

What changed my view was mostly watching what actually happened, and realizing my model was wrong about which axis mattered.

First, the thing I later wrote about as the "second half": once pretraining recipes and RL recipes converged across labs, the differentiator stopped being "who has the biggest model" and became "who has the best taste in problems and evaluation." Anthropic made a very narrow, very deliberate bet on coding and agents, long before it was obvious that bet would pay off. Coding is special. It's verifiable, it compounds, and developers are the people who decide which model everyone else ends up using. Claude Code is the clearest example. It wasn't the flashiest product, but it turned the model into something people live inside all day, and that feedback loop is worth more than a lot of compute.

Second, I underestimated how much culture matters in a world of agents. When a model is going to take actions on your behalf, write your code, touch your systems, the thing I had filed under "safety overhead" turns out to be the product. Reliability, honesty, not doing stupid destructive things: that's not a tax on capability, that's capability. Enterprises figured that out faster than I did.

And third, frankly, I was wrong about the economics. I assumed being compute-poor was fatal. It turned out that being focused is a decent substitute for being rich, at least for a while. If you only try to win one thing, you can win it with less.

So if you ask me now, I'd say my pessimism was a pretty standard first-half way of thinking, and Anthropic was one of the first labs to actually play the second half. I don't think I'd have put it that way when I left. It took watching the scoreboard for a year to update.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two things: believing in the team and believing in the company’s prospects. You can think the researchers are excellent and still worry about whether that translates into a sustainable business, especially when training frontier models requires so much capital and you’re competing with much larger companies.

But I’d be careful about reconstructing exactly what I thought when I left. Looking back, the assumption I’d question is that an early lead—or an advantage in distribution—necessarily becomes permanent. There’s room for a company to distinguish itself through the quality and usefulness of its models.

So I’m more open to Anthropic’s prospects now. The broader lesson for me is to be less confident in predictions about individual AI companies. The technology changes quickly enough that the assumptions behind those predictions can stop being true.
